newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian bomb explosion kills at least one.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian bomb explosion kills at least one.

text.p: A bomb blew up a Nigerian army bus inside a military camp in Lagos on Tuesday, killing at least one soldier and wounding 15 people, the third bombing against army targets in politically troubled Nigeria since December.
Witnesses said the bomb went off in a bus carrying soldiers inside an army camp in the Surulere district of Lagos and the area had been cordoned off by security authorities.
They said the death toll could be as high as six but a military spokesman disputed this.
"One person died, a soldier," Colonel Anthony Ugbo, the spokesman for defence headquarters, told Reuters.
"Investigations are going on. It is very unfortunate that this has happened at this time," he said.
Assistant police commissioner Mohammed Biu was quoted by the state news agency as saying the pattern of the blast was similar to the other recent explosions.
"We will try to find the people behind these explosions now that we can compare three different types in less than five weeks," Biu said.
Two bombs exploded within days last month clearly targeting the military administrator of Lagos state Colonel Muhammed Marwa, a close aide of military ruler General Sani Abacha.
Marwa was unhurt but about 20 soldiers were critically wounded in the two explosions.

Abacha's cabinet was meeting in the capital Abuja on Tuesday to consider the 1997 budget but was bound to discuss the blast 900 km (560 miles) south in Lagos, the bastion of opposition to his government.

Last month the U.S. State Department said in a statement that it had received information that bomb attacks might take place at Nigerian airports during the last two weeks of December and warned Americans travelling to the country to be cautious.

So far no one has claimed responsibility for the recent wave of bomb blasts in Nigeria but police say a bungled car bomb explosion in November that killed three people was the work of agents of exiled opposition leader Wole Soyinka.
Soyinka, winner of a Nobel Prize for literature, leads a group based abroad known as the National Liberation Council of Nigeria (NALICON) that has vowed to topple Abacha.
In an interview on BBC radio after the December bombings, Soyinka denied any involvement but refused to condemn the attacks.

State television reported on Monday night that authorities in neighbouring Benin had intercepted arms and ammunition that NALICON and NADECO, the umbrella opposition group the National Democratic Coalition to which it is allied, planned to smuggle into Nigeria.
Africa's most populous nation of 100 million slipped into turmoil in June 1993 when the then military president annulled an election to choose his successor and restore democracy.

Abacha, who came to power in the chaos that ensued, is implementing a programme he says will lead to the handover of power to a democratically elected president in October 1998 but his critics say his agenda is to stay in power.
They point to the continued detention of many opposition figures, among them Moshood Abiola, the wealthy businessman presumed to have won the annulled 1993 presidential poll.
On Monday the World Council of Churches (WCC) accused the government of widespread repression in Ogoniland.
The government has not yet reacted to the charges contained in a 106-page report compiled by senior WCC official Deborah Robinson during a secret visit to Nigeria in 1996.
